keyQuotes: I have now stopped writing most of the code myself and started acting like an engineering manager directing a team of agents.
The most common mistakes I see people make about delegation to both humans and agents are: asking for an action, not an outcome; not explaining the why; taking back control.
They're often designed to lock you into a particular vendor, when in reality you benefit a lot from being able to switch to whichever newer model works best, even if it comes from a different vendor.

mainPoints.explanation: Common mistakes are asking for an action instead of an outcome, not explaining the why, and taking back control after a mistake. The right approach is to give corrective feedback and let the agent improve.
mainPoints.point: Engineers should delegate to agents like managers delegate to junior engineers, focusing on outcomes and giving feedback.

mainPoints.explanation: High-quality speech recognition (e.g., OpenSuperWhisper running Whisper locally) lets you talk 3x faster than you type, applicable to prompting agents and any text input.
mainPoints.point: Voice input dramatically accelerates prompting and is a key productivity lever.

mainPoints.explanation: Using Lavish Editor, the agent renders a plan as an interactive HTML page that supports visual feedback, making iteration faster and more precise than editing markdown.
mainPoints.point: For complex work, create an interactive visual plan before handing off for autonomous implementation.

mainPoints.explanation: Avoid 'fancy gimmicks' like auto-managed memory that tie you to one provider; maintain the ability to switch models easily as better ones emerge.
mainPoints.point: Keep the agent stack agnostic to avoid vendor lock-in and retain flexibility.

mainPoints.explanation: Store explicit testing instructions in AGENTS.md per project, allowing the agent to run the real app and validate its own work before coming back to you.
mainPoints.point: Pre-define end-to-end validation instructions so agents can self-verify their changes.

oneSentenceSummary: A former Meta L8 engineer shares his complete agentic engineering setup—terminal-centric, keyboard-driven—using agents as autonomous teammates for planning, implementation, and validation.
originalTitle: An Ex-Meta L8’s Agentic Engineering Setup
summary: Kun Chen, ex-Meta L8 principal engineer, details his personal agentic engineering workflow that has enabled him to ship 30+ high-quality PRs per day. The setup is built entirely in the terminal: WezTerm, tmux, Neovim, and agent harnesses like Claude Code and OpenCode. Chen emphasizes writing prompts like a manager (asking for outcomes, not actions; explaining the why; giving feedback), using voice input for speed (OpenSuperWhisper), and planning complex work with interactive HTML artifacts via his open-source Lavish Editor. Implementation is fully autonomous once the plan is set, with agents validating their own changes end-to-end. The post uses a real project—'Hi Bit', an AI tutor for his son—as a concrete example.
title: An Ex-Meta L8’s Agentic Engineering Setup
